rv.q: Ray Davies' band was a poetic paradox and thus far more interesting theatrically than all of 'em.

Hearing these songs decomposed, rearranged and remixed is a true pleasure for anyone only passingly familiar with some of the bigger hits, and for the more seriously invested fans, the work that the musical team does here offers up the gift of a new and deeper appreciation for how well each holds up.
In all, “Sunny Afternoon” delivers a white-hot musical take on The Kinks.

The first act is crisp and engaging, demonstrating the fiery determination that both Ray and Dave possessed to get the band off the ground (as well as showing us the meet-cute between Ray and his first wife, Rasa).

It all adds up to a magnificently jubilant musical odyssey from the dominate opening riffs of Hoare’s “You Really Got Me” to “Lola,” “Waterloo Sunset” and a string of distinctive hits including “Just Can’t Sleep,” “Dedicated Follower of Fashion,” and “Too Much On My Mind/Tired of Waiting.”
SUNNY AFTERNOON is a vibrant musical tribute to The Kinks.
Stellar casting and a rocking score make Sunny Afternoon a theatrical event that you simply do not want to miss.
This jumping, jubilant jukebox musical is so much fun and a full evening (or a SUNNY AFTERNOON) overflowing with perfected performances and marvelous music.
Sunny Afternoon is an electrifying production and a tribute to the power and passion of rock and roll.
Sunny Afternoon is, in all the ways that count, a triumph.
And there is so much great music here (“Lola,” the title song, and “Till the End of the Day” among them) and clever, exuberant stagecraft that the relative thinness of the book hardly matters.
The performers are terrific and their renditions of the 30 or so songs is first-rate.
Ah well, a few missteps don't matter much when the music's this magnificent.
Whether it’s worth your while may depend on your general tolerance for bio-musicals.
Sunny Afternoon – based on the music of the Kinks, is an absolute blast!
Sunny Afternoon exceeds all of my expectations and gives us a story with so much drama, love, music that it feels like it can't be real.

This energetic jukebox musical, “Sunny Afternoon,” enjoying its North American premiere here in Chicago, is based on the story of the Kinks as told by lead singer and songster Ray Davies, filtered through the adept hand of playwright Joe Penhall.

cn.t: Critics enthusiastically embrace this energetic jukebox musical, praising its vibrant performances, particularly the talented leads, and the electrifying recreation of The Kinks' iconic catalog that brings the spirit of '60s rock to life.
